title: Teacher-written description 'My Grandfather's Workshop'
subject: English
source: Written for english/y6 lesson 81 (Teacher-written description 'My Grandfather's Workshop' (pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 81: What makes me me? Reading a description from a character's perspective (VIPERS). Read the ideas from the lesson, then do the tasks.

passage.title: Teacher-written description for TGA
paras: My grandfather speaks more with his hands than with his voice. In the workshop, sawdust settles on his sleeves like a fine snow, and he hums the same old tune he has hummed for sixty years. He measures twice and cuts once; he never rushes. When I ruined a table leg last spring, he simply handed me another piece of oak. "Wood forgives," he said, "if you are patient with it." I think he was talking about more than wood.

Evidence

model.title: What does 'I think he was talking about more than wood' suggest?

parts.text: Point: the advice is about people too
Evidence: 'Wood forgives... if you are patient'
Explain: he forgave the narrator's mistake
Link: the narrator has learned patience and forgiveness from him

parts.label: Why it works
parts.text: It suggests the grandfather's advice is about people: just as wood forgives, he forgave the narrator, teaching patience and forgiveness.

keywords.def: who a person is: their character, beliefs, history and what matters to them
the point of view a story is told from

questions.a: sawdust settles on his sleeves like a fine snow

questions.q: What does 'measures twice and cuts once' show?
How does the narrator feel about him?
Core: answer six VIPERS questions on the description
Extend: explain how the description would change if the grandfather told it himself
questions.a: For example: he might not call himself patient; we would learn his thoughts instead

questions.q: Stretch: what does this description suggest about identity?
questions.a: Identity shows in how we act and treat others, not just how we look

questions.q: Whose eyes do we see the grandfather through?
questions.a: C) his grandchild's. The narrator uses 'my grandfather' and 'I', so it is the grandchild.
